title: How learning works: the principles behind every technique
introHtml:
Most lasting learning comes from two habits: pulling information out of memory (retrieval) and doing it again at growing intervals (spacing). Everything else in this document either supports those two or makes them easier to keep up.

The seven principles below explain why. Once you understand them, you can judge any study method yourself, including ones this compendium does not mention: ask whether it makes you produce answers from memory, whether it spreads that effort over time, and whether it builds meaning rather than just familiarity.

items.title: Recognising is not remembering
items.leadHtml: Re-reading makes material feel familiar, and that feeling of fluency is easily mistaken for knowing it. The only real test is whether you can produce it with the book closed.

parts.why: Recognition and recall are different jobs. Recognising a face in a crowd is easy; drawing that face from memory is hard. When you re-read, the page supplies the answer and your brain only has to say "yes, I've seen this", which feels like knowing. In an exam, a conversation or a real task, nothing supplies the answer, and you need recall. The danger is that fluency (how easily something reads) is what your brain uses to judge how well you know it, and fluency comes cheaply from repetition.
parts.how:
1. After reading a section, close the source.
  2. Write or say the main points, or answer one question about it.
  3. Open the source and check. Only what you produced counts as known.

examples.simple: You read a recipe twice and it seems obvious. In the kitchen without the book, you cannot remember whether the butter goes in before or after the flour.
examples.nontrivial: A programmer reads a tutorial on recursion and every line makes sense. Asked to write a function that reverses a list recursively on a blank screen, she freezes. Following someone else's reasoning (recognition) is a different skill from building it yourself (recall), and only the second one transfers to new problems.

items.title: Forgetting is part of the process
items.leadHtml: Memory fades fast after first exposure (the forgetting curve). Each successful recall, especially when it takes some effort, makes the memory last longer.

parts.why: Picture a new memory as a leaky bucket. Right after you fill it, it leaks quickly; within a day much of it is gone. Each time you top it up by recalling, the bucket gets sturdier and leaks more slowly, so the next refill can wait longer. That is why review intervals can grow: 1 day, then 3, then a week, then a month. Retrieval also works like walking a path through a forest: the first walk is hard and the path barely shows, but each walk tramples it flatter, and a well-used path is easy to find even after weeks. Forgetting is not a sign you failed; a bit of forgetting before each review is what makes the next recall strengthen the path.
parts.how:
1. Expect to lose much of a new topic within a day or two. Plan the first review within 24 hours.
  2. Space later reviews further apart each time the recall succeeds.
  3. When recall fails, shorten the gap again.

examples.simple: You learn 20 Spanish words on Monday. By Tuesday you recall 9. After reviewing Tuesday, Thursday and the next Monday, you recall 18 a month later with only a few minutes of total work.
examples.nontrivial: A replication of Ebbinghaus's original experiment found the same steep early drop, and also a small bump in retention at 24 hours compared with shorter delays, plausibly because a night's sleep helped. The practical lesson: the first day matters most, and a review the next day catches material at the point where the bucket has leaked a lot but not emptied.

items.title: Desirable difficulties
items.leadHtml: Methods that feel harder in the moment (self-testing, spacing, mixing topics) produce better long-term memory than methods that feel smooth. A struggle to recall is a sign the method is working.

parts.why: Robert and Elizabeth Bjork distinguish two kinds of strength: how easily you can get at something right now (retrieval strength) and how deeply it is stored (storage strength). Easy practice boosts the first and barely touches the second. Effortful retrieval, when the memory is a bit faded, builds the second. It is like strength training: lifting a weight you can barely move builds muscle; lifting a feather a thousand times does not. The trap is that easy practice also feels better, so learners rate it as more effective.
parts.how:
1. Test yourself instead of re-reading.
  2. Leave gaps between study sessions on the same topic.
  3. Mix related topics or problem types in one session.
  4. Try to generate an answer before you look it up.

examples.simple: A tennis player who practises forehand, backhand and volley in a random mix feels clumsier in practice than one who hits 50 forehands in a row, but plays better in a match, where shots come in random order.
examples.nontrivial: In one study, people learned painters' styles either by seeing each painter's works grouped together or mixed with other painters. Mixed study led to better recognition of new paintings, yet most participants believed grouped study had helped them more, even after the test. A maths student faces the same trap: doing ten problems of one type in a row feels smooth, but mixing types forces you to practise choosing the method, which is what the exam asks.

items.title: Understanding before memorising
items.leadHtml: Facts tied to a mechanism ("why") are easier to keep and to use than isolated facts. Most subjects are cumulative: what you understand now carries into what you learn next.

parts.why: Memory is a web, not a list. A new fact that links to things you already know has many threads to hang from, so there are many routes back to it. An isolated fact hangs from one thread and drops easily. Understanding also lets you rebuild a forgotten detail: if you know why something happens, you can often work out the detail again. And because knowledge builds on itself (algebra into calculus, grammar into fluent writing, anatomy and physiology into pathology, pharmacology and clinical years in medicine), a weak foundation makes every later topic harder.
parts.how:
1. Before memorising details, make sure you can explain the main idea in two or three sentences.
  2. For each new fact, ask "why is this true?" and "how does it connect to what I know?".
  3. Only then put the details on cards.

examples.simple: Memorising that "the Romans built roads straight" is easy to forget. Knowing they were built to move armies quickly and to be easy to survey makes the fact stick and helps you guess other features of Roman roads.
examples.nontrivial: An economics student memorises "when interest rates rise, bond prices fall" and keeps mixing up the direction. Once he understands why (an old bond paying 2% is worth less when new bonds pay 4%, so its price must drop until its yield matches), he never confuses it again and can also reason about related cases he was never taught.

items.title: Generation beats consumption
items.leadHtml: Anything you produce yourself, such as an answer, a diagram, an explanation or a question, is remembered better than something you only read or watched.

parts.why: When you generate something, your brain has to search memory, choose, and build. That work leaves a stronger, more connected trace than passively receiving the finished product. It is the difference between being driven somewhere and driving there yourself: the passenger sees the same streets but the driver learns the route. A meta-analysis of the "generation effect" found a moderate, reliable advantage for generating over reading across many kinds of material.
parts.how:
1. Before reading the answer, try to produce it, even as a guess.
  2. Turn notes into questions and answer them.
  3. Draw the diagram from memory instead of copying it.
  4. Explain the idea in your own words, not the textbook's.

examples.simple: Completing "The capital of Australia is C_____" (Canberra) is remembered better than reading "The capital of Australia is Canberra".
examples.nontrivial: A student learning to play jazz piano transcribes a short solo by ear instead of reading a printed transcription. It takes ten times longer, but she remembers the phrases and can reuse them in her own playing. A history student who writes his own exam question on the causes of the First World War, then answers it, learns more than one who reads a model answer, because choosing what to ask already forces him to decide what matters.

items.title: Sleep consolidates memory
items.leadHtml: What you study is stabilised during sleep, so an all-nighter costs the very memories it was meant to build.

parts.why: During the day, new memories are held in a fragile, temporary form. During sleep, especially deep slow-wave sleep, the brain replays them and moves them into more lasting storage, like saving a draft document so it survives a restart. Sleep before learning matters too: after a night without sleep, the brain is worse at taking in new memories at all. So an all-nighter hurts twice: it weakens what you studied the day before and makes the next day's studying less effective.
parts.how:
1. Aim for 7 to 9 hours, at roughly regular times.
  2. Study the hardest new material earlier in the evening rather than late at night, then sleep.
  3. Before an exam, protect the night's sleep over one more late session.
  4. A short nap after learning can help when the night was short.

examples.simple: A child practising a new piano piece often plays it better the morning after than at the end of the evening's practice, without any extra practice in between.
examples.nontrivial: A student has a statistics exam at 9 am and three topics left. Staying up until 4 am to cover all three leaves her tired, slower at reasoning and with weaker memory of the earlier topics. Covering two topics well, sleeping 7 hours, and skimming the third over breakfast is the better bet, because sleep protects what she has already learned.

items.title: Cramming vs deep learning
items.leadHtml: Cramming works for an exam the next morning and fails a month later. Spaced retrieval takes about the same total time but is spread out, and it keeps working long after the exam.

parts.why: Cramming fills the leaky bucket to the brim right before the test, and for a few hours it holds. Then it leaks as fast as ever, because nothing made it sturdier. Spacing uses the same total time to refill the bucket several times, and each refill makes it leak more slowly. The cruel part is that cramming feels efficient: performance during a cram session is high, so it seems to work. Research on review gaps suggests a useful rule: the longer you need to remember something, the longer your gaps between reviews should be.
parts.how:
1. Split your total study time for a topic into several shorter sessions on different days.
  2. Start each session with recall of the earlier material before adding new.
  3. For an exam in a week, review every day or two; for an exam in a few months, space reviews a week or more apart.

examples.simple: Two students each spend 3 hours on a list of chemistry formulas. One spends 3 hours the night before; the other spends 30 minutes on six different days. Both pass the quiz. Only the second still knows the formulas in next term's course that assumes them.
examples.nontrivial: A law student needs case law both for the end-of-term exam and for the bar exam two years later. Cramming gets her through the first, but she will have to re-learn everything for the second. Spacing over the term costs no extra time now and leaves knowledge that only needs light review later. Knowledge you will build on (core maths, a language's grammar, basic sciences in medicine) is exactly what you should never cram.

If an exam is tomorrow and you have not started, cramming is better than nothing. Use active recall while you cram, and sleep for at least a few hours.
